title: Surface Tension: dyn/cm, mN/m and the Reason They Match
h1: Surface tension units — dyn/cm and mN/m
description: 1 dyn/cm = 1 mN/m exactly. Water is 72 mN/m at 20 °C. Mercury is 486 mN/m. Surface tension controls wetting, atomisation and coating thickness.

author.name: The Turbo Unit Converter engineering desk

reviewer.name: Turbo Unit Converter editorial review
reviewer.credential: verified against NIST SP 811 and category-specific ISO references

hero: Two units, one value. The CGS-to-SI switch happened to produce identical numeric values, and the industry stopped caring which name to use.
body: Surface tension is force per unit length along a fluid interface. Two systems of units happen to give identical numbers, which is why coating chemists and physicists speak past each other with no numerical harm.

> 1 dyn/cm = 1 mN/m = 10⁻³ N/m
> 1 N/m = 1000 mN/m = 1000 dyn/cm
Water: 72.8 mN/m. Ethanol: 22.4 mN/m. Mercury: 486 mN/m. Silicone oil (Dow 200): 20 mN/m. Molten aluminium: 914 mN/m. Air/vacuum: 0 by definition.

Wetting: contact angle set by γ_solid, γ_liquid, γ_interface (Young's equation). Coating thickness: capillary vs viscous forces (Landau–Levich). Ink-jet drop formation: Weber and Ohnesorge numbers. Surfactant selection: reduce γ to promote spreading.

Water sprayed through a 100 µm nozzle at 5 m/s. We = ρ v² d / γ = 1000 × 25 × 10⁻⁴ / 0.0728 = 34. Above We ≈ 12, bag breakup dominates — droplet size drops sharply. Reducing γ with a 0.5% surfactant to 30 mN/m raises We to 83 and pushes into sheet breakup.
Same number, two names. Water is 72 mN/m or dyn/cm.

faqs.a: Yes — it decreases roughly linearly with temperature and vanishes at the critical point.
Same units (mN/m), different interface — solid/liquid or liquid/liquid instead of liquid/gas.
